sentences.text: Ren listened to the boy every night for a week.
Sometimes Tetsuo talked about small things — his mother's cooking, a bird he had seen, a book he was reading.
Sometimes he only did the CQ and said his call sign and waited and then signed off.
He was never answered.
Ren wanted very badly to be able to answer.
He looked at the radio during the day and tried to understand if it might be modified to send.
It could not.
It was a receiver only.
One morning Obaachan came out to the porch where Ren was sitting.
She had two cups of tea.
She sat down next to him.
She was quiet for a moment.
Then she said, "You are listening to something on the radio.
Every night.
What are you listening to." Ren thought about lying.
He decided not to.
He said, "I think — I think I am hearing Ojiichan.
When he was a boy.
On the radio." Obaachan looked at him.
She did not laugh.
She did not say he was making it up.
She only nodded, very slowly.
"Can I listen with you," she said.
Ren said yes.
That night they sat together at the radio.
Ren tuned it to 6.185 exactly at midnight.
He handed Obaachan the headphones.
She put them on.
She closed her eyes.
She listened.
For a long time she did not say anything.
Ren could not hear what she was hearing, but he could see her face.
She was very still.
Once, her lips moved slightly, as if she was recognizing a word.
Once, she smiled — a very small smile, at nothing Ren could see.
Once, she took a breath in a way that Ren thought meant she was going to cry, but she did not.
She just breathed.
After twenty minutes she took the headphones off.
She set them down carefully on the tatami.
She sat very still.
Then she said, "That is his voice.
He was ten.
He was very serious as a boy.
He told me once about the time his teacher almost wrote a note home for drawing radios.
His father laughed and did not tell his mother.
That was the story he just told." She looked at Ren.
"I do not understand how this is happening.
But it is his voice.
And it is a night in maybe 1957.
He was ten in 1957."
Ren said, "Do you think it is real.
Or do you think — I don't know.
That it is us imagining something." Obaachan thought for a very long time.
Then she said, "I do not think it matters, Ren.
I think we are hearing him.
Whether it is a radio wave that has been bouncing around for seventy years and finally came back to us.
Or whether we are just remembering him, both of us together, so hard that we hear him.
It is the same thing.
He is here for a little while.
That is what is happening."
For the last few days of Ren's visit, they listened together every night.
They split the headphones — Obaachan wore one earpiece, Ren wore the other.
Sometimes Tetsuo told a story.
Sometimes he was quiet, and only did his CQ.
He never got an answer.
Ren wondered, sometimes, what would happen if someone — somewhere in the actual 1950s — had answered him.
He wondered if that had ever happened, in the real past.
He hoped it had.
On the last night — the night before Ren was going home — Obaachan turned to Ren, headphones between them.
She said, "He is going to say goodnight in a moment.
Then he will be gone.
And then we are going to have to move out of this house.
I do not know if we can hear him from the new apartment.
It might not work there.
It might be different.
So this may be the last night." Ren nodded.
He had thought about this too.
Tetsuo — Ojiichan, when he was a boy — did his sign-off in his slow careful voice.
Same time tomorrow, same frequency.
Over and out.
And then he was gone.
And there was only static.
Six weeks later, Ren went with his father to help Obaachan move.
They packed up everything, and Ren was allowed to carry the radio himself.
He carried it out to the moving truck in both arms, and he set it in a corner where it would not slide around.
Obaachan came out with the last of her boxes.
She stood in the driveway of the old house and looked at it for a while.
Then she got in the car with Ren's father.
The new apartment was smaller and cleaner and closer to the doctor.
There was no attic.
But Obaachan had a corner in the main room for the radio, and she put it there, on a low table where it could plug into the wall.
Ren was there the first night she tried it.
She turned it on at midnight.
She tuned it to 6.185.
She put the headphones on.
She listened for a long time.
Then she looked at Ren.
She smiled — a small strange smile.
"I can hear him," she said.
"He is here too.
Somehow." Ren was very glad.
He did not need to hear it himself.
He believed her.
And he understood, then, what Ojiichan had said once, according to Obaachan: that the radio was proof that people are less alone than they think.
That there are always voices in the air.
That you only had to know how to listen.
